subject: distance sampling to estimate density of invasive plants along

messages.author: 8380ad09cfe23c93
messages.subject: distance sampling to estimate density of invasive plants along
parts:
Hi everyone,

We are considering using distance sampling to estimate the density of 19
species of nonnative invasive plants along roads and trails within national
parks. The area of inference would be roads and trails (and a buffer
around them) because this is considered a high-risk area for weeds. A
different sampling approach will be applied to interior parklands.

Our concern is that the density of invasive plants along trails is
inversely related to distance from the trail, i.e., that objects are not
distributed in the area to be sampled according to some stochastic process,
and we'd like to be able to locate our sampling transects or point on the
trail. Given that a GRTS draw would be used to locate transects or points
along trails, is it absolutely necessary to randomly orient transects
and/or locate points in the buffered trail area? In many cases, thick
vegetation and steep topography make going off trail impractical. If we
are to use distance sampling, it would have to be from the road/trail.
Buckland et al. (2009) stated "more general methods of Buckland et al. (in
prep) allow estimation in these circumstances..... Fortunately, the bias
from this source is negligible for the large majority of studies."

Is there methodology that you can point us to in the Advanced Distance
Sampling book (it's in the mail)? Other suggestions?

Thanks for any assistance you can provide!

Stacey Ostermann-Kelm
NPS Inventory & Monitoring Program
